Horses have a huge fermentation vat in their large intestine—the cecum and colon. This part of the digestive tract is packed with billions of bacteria, protozoa, and fungi. These microbes produce enzymes that can break down cellulose and other complex carbohydrates that humans (and most mammals) can’t digest.

### 2. Microbes turn fiber into protein
As the microbes break down the fibrous plant matter, they grow and multiply using the carbon and energy from that fiber. To build their own cells, they incorporate nitrogen from the diet (even the small amount of protein in forage) and from urea recycled into the gut via the horse’s blood. The microbes essentially synthesize all the essential amino acids and build complete protein.

### 3. The horse digests the microbes themselves
Once the microbial population grows in the hindgut, some of those microbes flow out with the digesta and are digested in the lower gut. The horse’s enzymes break down the microbial cells, absorbing their amino acids, vitamins, and other nutrients. In this way, the horse gets a steady supply of high‑quality microbial protein—even if the original forage was low in protein.

### 4. Horses also get protein directly from forage
Contrary to the myth that horses eat only straw, they normally eat grass, hay, or legume forages (alfalfa, clover), which contain 8–20% protein. Even when they consume lower-quality roughage like straw, the microbial protein fills the gap. Horses do need a certain amount of dietary protein, and working horses, pregnant mares, or growing foals are often supplemented with extra protein sources (soybean meal, etc.) beyond what microbes alone can provide.

### Why can’t humans do this?
Humans are monogastric with only a very limited microbial fermentation in the large intestine. We don’t have a specialized chamber like the horse’s cecum to host a massive microbial population, and we cannot digest the microbes in large enough quantities to meet our protein needs. Our gut absorbs nutrients mainly in the small intestine, so we depend on directly eating protein that we can break down into amino acids. We lack the ability to recycle urea into the gut on a large scale to feed microbes, and we can’t extract significant energy from cellulose.

### The bottom line
A horse’s massive muscles aren’t built from straw—they’re built from the microbial protein that the horse’s gut “grows” from fiber, plus the natural protein in the grasses and hay it eats. It’s a beautiful example of symbiosis: the horse provides the fiber and a stable environment, and the microbes provide the protein and energy in return.
